examples.solution_text:
The outlier is $(1,10)$: it lies far above the upward trend of the other points.

It pulls the low-$x$ end of the fitted line upward, flattening it. Removing it makes the gradient more positive and steeper.

The outlier is $(6,12)$: it lies far above the main upward trend.

It pulls the high-$x$ end upward, making the fitted line steeper than the remaining trend. Removing it makes the gradient less steep; it remains positive.

The outlier is $(6,11)$: it lies far above the downward trend of the other points.

It pulls the right-hand end upward, flattening the downward line. Removing it makes the gradient more negative and steeper.

The outlier is $(1,13)$.

It pulls the low-$x$ end upward, making the downward fitted line steeper than the trend of the remaining points. Removing it makes the gradient less negative and less steep.

The effect depends on the outlier's position relative to the main trend.

methods.description: Identify a point far from the main trend and read its coordinates.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Data Analysis B_Bivariate Data.md lines 465–501, Drawing a Line of Best Fit, Development questions 4–5

methods.description: Compare a positive fitted line with the remaining upward trend; removal of a flattening outlier makes the gradient more positive.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Data Analysis B_Bivariate Data.md lines 465–490 and 509–521, Drawing a Line of Best Fit, Development questions 4 and 6

methods.description: Use the outlier's position to recognise an upward pull at high x; removing that point makes a positive gradient less steep.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Data Analysis B_Bivariate Data.md lines 1827–1846, Pearson's r value, Mastery question 13; adapt its graphical gradient-change reasoning with removal reversing the added point's effect

methods.description: Recognise an outlier flattening a downward line; removal makes the gradient more negative and steeper.
methods.sourceRef: booklets/mathsmap-sources/Stage 5/Data Analysis B_Bivariate Data.md lines 492–507, Drawing a Line of Best Fit, Development question 5

methods.description: Compare a downward fitted line with the remaining trend; removing a high point at low x makes the gradient less negative and less steep.

coverage.summary: Authored four worked examples covering identification and both steepening and flattening for positive and negative gradients. Used different data, editable TikZ, black ordinary diagram ink, standard blue fitted lines, 10 pt ordinary labels and 8.5 pt ticks. All lines stay within their data's horizontal range. Solutions remain editable prose and inherit the renderer's blue; no calculation gutters are needed. Accepted assessments were classified by method only and were neither changed nor re-audited. Independent review and final-size visual verification remain for the coordinator.

examples.derivation: The six remaining points lie on y=x+1. The point (1,10) is clearly outside this trend. Independently fitting all seven points gives y=0.25x+4.5, matching the drawn endpoints (1,4.75) and (6,6). Removal increases the gradient from 0.25 to 1: more positive and steeper. This adapts the graphical reasoning in booklet lines 509–521 and image39.

The six remaining points lie on y=x+1; (6,12) lies above that trend. Independently fitting all seven points gives y=1.46875x-0.09375, matching the drawn endpoints (1,1.375) and (6,8.71875). Removal decreases the gradient to 1, leaving it positive but less steep. Booklet lines 1827–1846 and image121 support reasoning about a high-x point above the trend steepening the line; removal reverses that effect.

The six remaining points lie on y=9-x; (6,11) lies far above the downward trend. Independently fitting all seven points gives y=7.25-0.25x, matching the drawn endpoints (1,7) and (6,5.75). Removal changes the gradient from -0.25 to -1, making it more negative and steeper. This matches the taught graphical comparison in booklet lines 492–507 and image38.

The six remaining points lie on y=9-x; (1,13) lies above the trend at low x. Independently fitting all seven points gives y=11.1875-1.46875x, matching the drawn endpoints (1,9.71875) and (6,2.375). Removal changes the gradient to -1, making it less negative and less steep. This is a valid adaptation of the position-and-trend comparison taught in booklet lines 465–521 and images35–39, without introducing regression calculation as a student task.

review.summary: All 22 exact assessment locators are mapped consistently, covering identification and positive/negative gradient steepening or flattening. Four examples cover every mapped method using different values and booklet-supported graphical reasoning. No existing examples require retention or disposition. Separate prompt and solution fields preserve hidden answers; editable prose inherits blue solution styling. No relation-led calculations require phantom gutters. Diagrams use appropriate editable TikZ, standard colours, specified label sizes and lines confined to the data range. No syllabus exception or solid-geometry review is required. Accepted practice and quiz mathematics was not re-audited. Actual rendering and final-size typography remain for the coordinator’s visual stage.
